                                  15   II.    INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE
                                  16          Before deciding the motion to dismiss, the Court must set the scope of the record. In

                                  17   general, a court may not consider material beyond the pleadings when ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6)

                                  18   motion. Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, 899 F.3d 988, 998 (9th Cir. 2018). The only exceptions

                                  19   to this rule are documents that are the subject of judicial notice, appended to the complaint, or

                                  20   incorporated by reference. Id.

                                  21          The Court previously ruled that invoices for the Centura and Epsilon systems were

                                  22   incorporated by reference. 2026 Order at 4. The Motion cites those same invoices. See Epicrew

                                  23   Contracts, ECF Nos. 74-1, 74-2. These documents were not appended to the complaint. See SAC.

                                  24   But they are incorporated by reference because they “form the basis of” Plaintiff’s contract claims:

                                  25   Plaintiff claims that Defendants breached these contracts. Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1002.

                                  26   Consequently, the Court will consider the contracts.

                                       III.    MOTION TO DISMISS
                                   1
                                               A.      Legal Standard
                                   2
                                                       1.       Rule 12(b)(6)
                                   3
                                               A complaint must contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the
                                   4
                                       pleader is entitled to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2). A defendant may move to dismiss a
                                   5
                                       complaint for failing to state a claim upon which relief can be granted under Rule 12(b)(6). When
                                   6
                                       deciding whether to grant a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), the court must generally accept
                                   7
                                       as true all “well-pleaded factual allegations.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 664 (2009).
                                   8
                                       Plaintiffs need not offer detailed factual allegations to meet this standard, but they are required to
                                   9
                                       offer “sufficient factual matter . . . ‘to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Id. at
                                  10
                                       678 (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). The court must construe the
                                  11
                                       alleged facts and inferences in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. See Retail Prop. Trust v.
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       United Bd. of Carpenters & Joiners of Am., 768 F.3d 938, 945 (9th Cir. 2014) (“[The court] must
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       accept as true all factual allegations in the complaint and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of
                                  14
                                       the nonmoving party.”). However, “courts are not bound to accept as true a legal conclusion
                                  15
                                       couched as a factual allegation.” Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678.
                                  16
                                                       2.       Rule 9(b)
                                  17
                                               Additionally, claims sounding in fraud must meet the heightened pleading requirements of
                                  18
                                       Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b). See Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1102–
                                  19
                                       03 (9th Cir. 2003). Under Rule 9(b), a party “must state with particularity the circumstances
                                  20
                                       constituting fraud.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b). Typically, Rule 9(b) requires the party alleging fraud to
                                  21
                                       plead “the who, what, when, where, and how” of the misconduct. Vess, 317 F.3d at 1106 (quoting
                                  22
                                       Cooper v. Pickett, 137 F.3d 616, 627 (9th Cir. 1997)).

                                               B.      Discussion
                                  24
                                                       1.       All Causes of Action as to Individual Defendants
                                  25
                                               Plaintiff’s FAC added Defendants Jacob, Gill, and Ruiz as defendants. Plaintiff alleged
                                  26
                                       that the Individual Defendants “intentionally undercapitalized CAE to perpetrate fraud while

                                   1   avoiding personal liability to creditors such as Epicrew,” “misused corporate funds for their own

                                   2   benefit,” and “authorized, directed, and/or participated in the fraudulent conduct.” FAC ¶¶ 45, 82.

                                   3   The Court found that Plaintiff had failed to plead that the Individual Defendants were liable

                                   4   through alter ego or direct liability and dismissed all claims against those defendants. 2026 Order

                                   5   at 7.

                                   6             The SAC makes the same allegations against the Individual Defendants, SAC ¶¶ 63–65,

                                   7   but adds four statements made by Defendant Gill after Plaintiff purchased the Centura system. Id.

                                   8   ¶¶ 32, 35, 40, 55.

                                   9                            a.      Alter Ego Theory of Liability
                                  10             Plaintiff argues that the Individual Defendants should be held liable as alter egos of Capital

                                  11   Asset. The SAC adds the allegation that on December 19, 2023, Defendant Gill emailed Plaintiff

                                  12   stating, “My main role is managing the operations of our 350 employee firm . . . I’ll be online for
Northern District of California

                                  13   another few hours ensuring our business continues, and the other 500 active shipments reach their

                                  14   destinations successfully and compliantly, by ensuring the various departments and employees

                                  15   involved are doing what is required . . .” SAC ¶ 55. In moving to dismiss, Defendants contend

                                  16   that Gill’s management role alone does not render him an alter ego of Capital Asset. Mot. at 8.

                                  17             Alter ego liability holds a person liable for the actions of their sham corporation. Leek v.

                                  18   Cooper, 194 Cal. App. 4th 399, 417–18 (2011). To plead alter ego liability, the plaintiff must

                                  19   show (1) that there is such a “unity of interest” between the corporation and individual that they

                                  20   are not “separate personalities” and (2) that treating the conduct at issue as the corporation’s alone

                                  21   would lead to an “inequitable result.” Mesler v. Bragg Management Co., 39 Cal.3d 290, 300

                                  22   (1985).

                                  23             Plaintiff has pled neither of these two elements. The mere fact that Defendant Gill

                                  24   managed operations for a 350-person firm does not establish a unity of interest. Indeed, even

                                  25   “controlling a corporation . . . does not give rise to alter ego liability; otherwise, every company

                                  26   would be an alter ego of its CEO and managers.” Smith v. Lanza, No. 21-CV-08785-JST, 2022

                                   1   WL 20243472, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 18, 2022); see also Katzir’s Floor & Home Design, Inc. v.

                                   2   M-MLS.com, 394 F.3d 1143, 1149 (9th Cir. 2004) (“The mere fact of sole ownership and control

                                   3   does not eviscerate the separate corporate identity that is the foundation of corporate law.”). And

                                   4   Plaintiff does not plead any additional facts that would establish a unity of interest for Defendants

                                   5   Jacob and Ruiz. Consequently, the Court again finds that Plaintiff has failed to plead that

                                   6   Defendants Jacob, Gill, and Ruiz should be liable as alter egos.

                                   7                           b.      Direct Liability as Corporate Officers
                                   8            Corporate officers are personally liable for torts they commit or direct. PMC, Inc. v.

                                   9   Kadisha, 78 Cal. App. 4th 1368, 1381–82 (2000). First, Defendants argue that the SAC does not

                                  10   allege any facts indicating that Defendants Jacob or Ruiz are personally liable for the allegedly

                                  11   fraudulent conduct. Mot. at 8–9. The Court agrees. Plaintiff contends that “it strains credulity to

                                  12   suggest that a fraudulent scheme . . . was executed without the knowledge and direction of its
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   CEO and Managing Director,” but as the Court noted in its previous order, Plaintiff must at least

                                  14   state the facts on which that belief is founded. 2026 Order at 6–7 (citing Moore v. Kayport

                                  15   Package Exp., Inc., 885 F.2d 531, 540 (9th Cir. 1989)). Plaintiff has added no such facts to the

                                  16   SAC, so the Court finds that Defendants Jacob and Ruiz are not personally liable for any alleged

                                  17   fraud.

                                  18            Plaintiff did, however, plead additional facts in an attempt to establish Defendant Gill’s

                                  19   liability for the alleged fraud. Three of those statements were regarding the Centura system. On

                                  20   November 28, 2023, Defendant Gill emailed Epicrew, stating, “I oversee [Capital Asset]’s global

                                  21   operations. . . . I see that our team is working diligently to push all parties involved to complete

                                  22   removal and make the equipment ready for export. I’ll personally see if I can assist in the

                                  23   expediting of remaining steps.” SAC ¶ 32. On December 15, 2023, Defendant Gill emailed

                                  24   saying that he would “meet with the team today to get a proper update.” SAC ¶ 35. On December

                                  25   19, 2023, Defendant Gill wrote, “I’ve been informed that we can expect the equipment to be

                                  26   crated and shipped in the second week of January.” SAC ¶ 40. On the same day, Defendant Gill

                                   1   also responded to Plaintiff’s request for an update on the Epsilon system, stating, “My main role is

                                   2   managing the operations of our 350 employee firm . . . I’ll be online for another few hours

                                   3   ensuring our business continues, and the other 500 active shipments reach their destinations

                                   4   successfully and compliantly, by ensuring the various departments and employees involved are

                                   5   doing what is required . . .” SAC ¶ 55.

                                   6           Defendants contend that the timing of these statements could not have induced Plaintiff’s

                                   7   purchase of either the Centura or the Epsilon system. Mot. at 8–9. Defendant Gill made the

                                   8   statements regarding the Centura system on November 28, December 15, and December 19, 2023,

                                   9   more than six months after Plaintiff purchased the Centura system. SAC ¶¶ 32, 35, 40. And

                                  10   Defendant Gill made the Epsilon statement on December 19, thirteen days after Plaintiff

                                  11   purchased the Epsilon. SAC ¶ 55. Thus, the Centura statements could not have induced Plaintiff

                                  12   to buy the Centura system, and the Epsilon statement could not have induced Plaintiff to buy the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Epsilon system.

                                  14           Resisting this conclusion, Plaintiff insists that the statements were part of “a continuing

                                  15   fraud” intended to “extend and conceal the original fraud by preventing Epicrew from discovering

                                  16   the truth and pursuing its rights.” Opp. at 6. Essentially, the argument is that the statements

                                  17   induced Plaintiff to continue relying on the two contracts. But in a fraud claim, the continuation

                                  18   of an alleged fraud alone does not constitute damages. A plaintiff “cannot base its fraudulent

                                  19   inducement allegations on promissory fraud that occurred after the parties had already entered into

                                  20   the . . . agreement . . . because it does not allege that . . . the statements induced anything other

                                  21   than continued performance on the agreement.” See Juice Roll-Upz, Inc. v. Liquid Guys

                                  22   Distributions, Inc., No. SACV 17-2052-JVS, 2018 WL 6118606, at *5 n.1 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 2,

                                  23   2018). Consequently, Plaintiff has failed to plead that Defendant Gill is personally liable for any

                                  24   alleged fraud arising from the Centura or Epsilon transactions.

                                  26           In sum, Plaintiff has not adequately pled that any of the Individual Defendants are liable

                                   1   either under a theory of alter ego or direct liability. Courts “should freely give leave [to amend]

                                   2   when justice so requires.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2); In re Korean Air Lines Co., Ltd., 642 F.3d

                                   3   685, 701 (9th Cir. 2011). But here, Plaintiff has had multiple opportunities to name the Individual

                                   4   Defendants and to allege facts to support liability, but Plaintiff has not done so. Consequently, the

                                   5   Court DISMISSES all claims against the Individual Defendants WITHOUT LEAVE to amend.

                                   6   With the Individual Defendants dismissed, the Court will consider the rest of the motion only with

                                   7   respect to Capital Asset.

                                   8                  2.      Fraud and Intentional Misrepresentation (Counts III and V)
                                   9          Plaintiff alleges that Capital Asset made misrepresentations that led Plaintiff to believe

                                  10   Defendants were in control of the Centura and Epsilon systems. SAC ¶¶ 91–98. As to the

                                  11   Centura system, Plaintiff claims that three statements—that Capital Asset had “just secured” the

                                  12   Centura system, that “the tool has an immediate release date, but it typically takes around 3–4
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   weeks on the supplier side to arrange removal,” and “[y]our purchase has been approved . . . our

                                  14   logistics team will be reaching out to you . . . to start the tool removal process”—led Plaintiff to

                                  15   believe that Capital Asset controlled the Centura system. Id. ¶¶ 19, 21, 25. Plaintiff also claims

                                  16   the Centura sales literature was “misleading.” Id. ¶ 95. As to the Epsilon system, Plaintiff alleges

                                  17   that the statements that “[Capital Asset] would like to finalize the removal and preparation for

                                  18   shipment” but would “need a remittance receipt,” the equipment “is being shipped to Epicrew

                                  19   from Singapore,” and “we can expect the equipment to be crated and shipped in the second week

                                  20   of January” led Plaintiff to believe that Capital Asset controlled the system. Id. ¶¶ 48–49, 40.

                                  21          The elements of fraud are (1) a misrepresentation, (2) knowledge of falsity, (3) an intent to

                                  22   defraud, (4) justifiable reliance, and (5) resulting damages. Lazar v. Superior Court, 12 Cal. 4th

                                  23   631, 638 (1996). The Court will consider whether Plaintiff has pled the elements of fraud for each

                                  24   of the statements.

                                  25                          a.      “Just Secured” Statement
                                  26          Plaintiff alleges that on May 23, 2023, Capital Asset stated it had “just secured” the

                                   1   Centura system. SAC ¶ 91. The SAC alleges that this statement led Plaintiff to believe that

                                   2   Capital Asset owned the Centura system, which induced Plaintiff to sign the purchase invoice and

                                   3   wire money to Capital Asset. Id. ¶¶ 25, 94.

                                   4                                  i.       Misrepresentation
                                   5          First, the Court considers whether Plaintiff has alleged that the “just secured” statement

                                   6   was false. Capital Asset contends that Plaintiff has not done so. Mot. at 10.

                                   7          A claim of fraud made on information and belief must be accompanied by a statement of

                                   8   facts on which that belief is founded. Shroyer v. New Cingular Wireless Servs., Inc., 622 F.3d

                                   9   1035, 1042 (9th Cir. 2010). Here, Plaintiff has done just that, pleading that for months after the

                                  10   sale, Capital Asset failed to deliver the equipment or even offer an estimated delivery date. SAC

                                  11   ¶¶ 30–40. From these facts, Plaintiff infers that Capital Asset had not secured the equipment when

                                  12   this statement was made. The Court is required to draw all reasonable inferences in favor of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Plaintiff, so the Court concludes that Plaintiff has adequately pled a misrepresentation. Retail

                                  14   Prop. Trust, 768 F.3d at 945 (9th Cir. 2014).

                                  15                                  ii.      Knowledge of Falsity and Intent to Defraud
                                  16          Second, the Court considers whether Plaintiff has adequately pled both knowledge of

                                  17   falsity and an intent to defraud. On information and belief, Plaintiff alleges that the solicitation of

                                  18   the purchase was a “calculated effort to extract payment with no corresponding intent to perform.”

                                  19   Id. ¶ 44. Here again, Defendant contends Plaintiff has not pled facts on which this belief is based.

                                  20   Mot. at 14–15. But Plaintiff alleges that Capital Asset required full advance payment, SAC ¶ 27,

                                  21   and that other companies have sued Capital Asset for the same or similar alleged schemes, id. ¶¶

                                  22   67–69. From this, Plaintiff infers that Capital Asset knew it had not secured the Centura system

                                  23   but intentionally led Plaintiff to believe that it had. The Court finds that Plaintiff has pled

                                  24   sufficient facts to support this inference and consequently concludes that Plaintiff has pled

                                  25   knowledge of falsity and intent to defraud.

                                   1          Third, the Court considers whether Plaintiff has adequately pled justifiable reliance. In

                                   2   moving to dismiss, Capital Asset argues that Section 5 of the Epicrew Contracts—which states

                                   3   “[a]ll Equipment is offered to Buyer based on its prior sale to [Capital Asset]”—makes it clear that

                                   4   when Capital Asset made the “just secured” statement, it did not yet own the Centura System. In

                                   5   Opposition, Plaintiff posits that Section 5 should not apply because “[a] party cannot immunize

                                   6   itself from liability for intentional misrepresentation through a contractual provision.” Opp. at 8

                                   7   (citing Manderville v. PCG&S Group, Inc., 146 Cal. App. 4th 1486, 1500 (2007)).

                                   8          California Civil Code Section 1668 provides that “[a]ll contracts which have for their

                                   9   object, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for his own fraud . . . are

                                  10   against the policy of the law.” Cal. Civ. Code § 1668. A party to a contract cannot relieve herself

                                  11   of liability simply by placing an exculpatory clause into the contract. Manderville, 146 Cal. App.

                                  12   4th at 1501. But here, Section 5 does not aim to waive liability. Rather, Section 5 merely
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   “implied the ‘possibility . . . that Capital Asset did not own the relevant equipment at the time.’”

                                  14   2026 Order at 12 (citing 2025 Order at 5–6); but cf. Simmons v. Ratterree Land Co., 217 Cal. 201,

                                  15   203 (1932) (finding that a provision that the buyer did not rely on extra-contractual representations

                                  16   did not exempt seller from liability for misrepresentations that induced the buyer to contract);

                                  17   Smith v. Rickards, 149 Cal. App. 2d 648, 653 (1957) (similar). Consequently, the Section 5

                                  18   statement is not against public policy.

                                  19          The Court thus reads the “just secured” statement in light of Section 5. Section 5 states

                                  20   that if Capital Asset was not able to purchase the equipment from a manufacturer, then any further

                                  21   contract to sell that equipment would be null and void. Epicrew Contracts at 1. When Capital
